title: Nothing great without enthusiasm
hook: nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm (Circles)

segments.voice: Yesterday, around every circle: Emerson's claim that around every circle another can be drawn. Your line was another circle. Where did your view get a little wider? Day one thousand two hundred two.

Same essay, last page. Emerson has spent all of Circles saying that nothing stays settled. Every idea gets outgrown. Every wall turns out to have a door in it. A reader can come out of it a little dizzy, wondering what is left to stand on. And then, near the close, he sets down one sentence like a flag in the ground: "Nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm." Not talent. Not a plan. Not the right people. Enthusiasm. It's a word that can sound like a pep rally, or a job listing asking for an enthusiastic self-starter. Emerson means something larger and stranger than that. Today, his word.
screen: `NOTHING STAYS SETTLED.` → `A FLAG IN THE GROUND.` → `NOT A PEP RALLY.`

segments.voice: First, where the line sits. Just before it, Emerson describes what he thinks people want more than almost anything: to forget ourselves for a while, to be surprised out of our good manners, to do something without knowing how or why. In his words, "to draw a new circle." So enthusiasm, for him, is the force that carries a person past the edge of the old circle. Second, it's a kind of letting go. Right after the line, Emerson says the way of life goes by abandonment. Not careful steps, but being taken over by something. A musician who stops counting and starts playing. A child so deep in a sandcastle that dinner is called three times. That absorption is what he's pointing at. Third, it isn't noise. Enthusiasm in this sense can be very quiet. A gardener on her knees at dawn, completely inside the work, may have more of it than someone shouting at a game. The test isn't volume. It's whether the self-watching part of you has gone quiet because the thing in front of you is bigger. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary Tuesday. A lot of a day can be done at half power, one eye on the clock, one eye on how we look. Emerson's claim is that nothing great comes out of that state. Small things can be done the other way too: a meal, a letter, a walk, a conversation, given the whole of you for a few minutes.
screen: `TO DRAW A NEW CIRCLE.` · `THE WAY OF LIFE IS ABANDONMENT.` · `ENTHUSIASM CAN BE QUIET.` · `NOT AT HALF POWER.` · then, large: `NOTHING GREAT WITHOUT ENTHUSIASM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to do one thing with enthusiasm. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one ordinary thing you'll do today. Washing a pan. Answering a message. Walking to the car. Picture yourself doing it with your whole attention, the way the child is inside the sandcastle. Notice how the hands would move, what you'd see, what you'd hear. No forced cheer needed. Just all of you, for the length of one small task. The bell holds the time.
Nothing great without enthusiasm. The line near the end of Emerson's Circles: the force that carries us past the old circle, by letting go rather than holding back. Today's word.
Your line: with enthusiasm. Pick the one small task you pictured, and when it comes, do it with your whole self, even if it takes two minutes. Day one thousand two hundred two.

howItsDone: Readers of Emerson often quote this line from Circles alongside the passage just before it, about the wish to forget ourselves and draw a new circle, as a call to throw oneself fully into work and life.
